# A #[foreign] mark says what to emit, not what a type is. Several SNGL types
# map to one target-language type — int8 and int16 are both a JS number — so a
# marked declaration is its own type: it does not become the imported
# declaration whose triple it repeats, and two marks with one triple do not
# become each other.

# Control: the same declaration is still the same type, so nothing here rejects
# a foreign-marked struct on its own.
sngl check ok.sngl
stdout 'ok.sngl: ok'

# Two marks, one triple, two types.
! sngl check twomarks.sngl
stderr 'cannot pass A as B'

# A mark and the js:// import it names: still two types.
! sngl check markvsimport.sngl
stderr 'cannot pass Entry as'

-- ok.sngl --
import . "sngl://std"

#[foreign("js://example.com/api", "Entry")]
struct A {
    title string
}

func take(a A) => a.title

component main {
    text(value=take(A{title="x"}))
}

-- twomarks.sngl --
import . "sngl://std"

#[foreign("js://example.com/api", "Entry")]
struct A {
    title string
}

#[foreign("js://example.com/api", "Entry")]
struct B {
    title string
}

func take(b B) => b.title

component main {
    text(value=take(A{title="x"}))
}

-- markvsimport.sngl --
import . "sngl://std"
import api "js://./api"

#[foreign("js://./api", "Entry")]
struct Entry {
    title string
}

func take(e api.Entry) => e.title

component main {
    text(value=take(Entry{title="x"}))
}
-- api/index.ts --
export type Entry = { title: string };
export function nothing(): number { return 0; }
